paras: The threatened lynching of Benjamin Pugh took place in Brooklyn, New York, on the afternoon of August 23, 1900, when a crowd that gathered at his arrest shouted "Lynch him!" as police led away Pugh, a Black man accused of shooting and killing a white waiter, John Tietjen. Police took Pugh to the station unharmed, and he was arraigned for first-degree murder and held for the grand jury. New York papers covered the case in detail, a Washington paper headed its dispatch "A Lynching Averted," and a Richmond editorial used it to argue that the North was facing "the negro question."

Pugh, 25, lived at 672 Gates Avenue and worked for the Stonington steamboat line. Tietjen, who had a wife and four children, waited tables in a restaurant at 1719 Fulton Street, where Pugh came in for lunch a little after 1 o'clock. In the Tribune's telling, Tietjen took the order "in a haughty manner," and when Pugh threw down two nickels for his 10-cent meal, the waiter sprang at him and kicked him. The Sun said instead that Pugh started to leave without paying, brushed the coins onto the floor, and was made to pick them up before Tietjen "hustled him out."

After leaving the restaurant, Pugh bought a revolver, according to both local accounts, at a Fulton Street hardware store, returned to challenge Tietjen to fight, and fired four shots, two of which killed the waiter on the spot. Fireman Peter J. Keenan, passing on a trolley car, chased him into the house at 20 Marion Street. There Keenan held him until Policeman Summergill arrived and made the arrest, though the Sun added that Pugh first drew a knife on the fireman.

By then a large crowd had gathered, about three hundred people by the Tribune's estimate, and a patrol wagon brought six more patrolmen. As Pugh was brought out, the crowd cried "Lynch him!" and, in the Sun's version, "Lynch the nigger!" The Tribune reported "no concerted attempt to harm the prisoner" and said the crowd fell back when a policeman drew a revolver. Pugh, "trembling with fear" according to the Sun, reached the station without violence, admitted the shooting, and said Tietjen had assaulted him and he had only protected himself.

On August 24 Pugh was arraigned before Magistrate Teale in the Gates Avenue police court on a charge of first-degree murder, and a crowd outside the building hooted at him. His lawyer entered a plea of not guilty, and as he left for the Raymond Street Jail he allegedly said, "I thought a colored man had as much right to defend himself as a white man." On August 27 Teale held him for the action of the grand jury; no report of an indictment or trial was found in the coverage.

The Evening World reported the shooting the same afternoon as "NEGRO SHOT WAITER DEAD," spelling the accused man's name "Puglis" and saying nothing of a crowd. The next morning the Tribune ran "NEGRO KILLS A WAITER" with a deck reading "CROWD THREATEN TO LYNCH ASSAILANT," calling the killing premeditated. The Sun's "NEGRO MURDERS A WAITER" called Pugh "the murderer" and printed the crowd's slur without comment.

Outside New York, the Washington Times carried the Sun's account as "A LYNCHING AVERTED," while papers in New Haven and Worcester ran a short wire item that blamed slow service and said Pugh made no attempt to escape, contradicting the local reports of a chase. The Richmond Times retold the Tribune story in an editorial, "TWO STORIES FROM NEW YORK," tying it to "the recent race riots in that city" and remarking that "when you get a negro and a gun in combination you may look out for trouble." All of the coverage found came from white dailies; no Black-press report of the case was found.

Accounts of the quarrel differ: the Tribune said Tietjen kicked Pugh, while the Sun quoted witnesses who said Tietjen made no attempt to assault him when the shots were fired; Pugh claimed self-defense.

accounts.gist: Tietjen served Pugh haughtily and kicked him after Pugh threw down two nickels; Pugh bought a revolver, returned, and shot him; a crowd of about 300 cried 'Lynch him!' but fell back when a policeman drew a revolver.

accounts.label: Sun local account and Washington dispatch
accounts.gist: Pugh tried to leave without paying and brushed coins to the floor; Tietjen made him pick them up and hustled him out; after the shooting Pugh drew a knife on Keenan; the crowd cried 'Lynch him!' 'Lynch the nigger!' but he reached the station unharmed.

accounts.label: Pugh's own claim
accounts.gist: Pugh admitted the shooting but said Tietjen had assaulted him and he had only protected himself.

accounts.label: Short wire report
accounts.gist: A dispute over slow service led Pugh to shoot the waiter; he made no attempt to escape and was locked up; no crowd is mentioned.

framing.detail: The Tribune headed it 'NEGRO KILLS A WAITER' with a deck on the crowd's threat, called the murder 'premeditated', yet described the waiter's 'haughty manner' at serving a Black man.
The Sun's 'NEGRO MURDERS A WAITER' called Pugh 'the murderer', printed the crowd's slur, and noted 'Demonstration by the Crowd' without comment.
The Washington Times ran the New York account as 'A LYNCHING AVERTED'; New England papers ran a short wire item ('Impatient Negro', 'Shot a Slow Waiter') with no crowd.

The Richmond Times editorial treated the case as proof that 'when you get a negro and a gun in combination you may look out for trouble' and that the North was learning the 'negro question', while noting officers kept the threatened lynching from happening.
